claim: All active TEs in the chicken germ line are targeted by piRNAs.
source: Here we reported that all active TEs in the chicken germ line are targeted by piRNAs, and as TEs lose their activity, the corresponding piRNAs erode away.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding directly in the abstract, and Figure 2B shows that all 73 actively expressed TE families are targeted by piRNAs (Fisher's exact test, p<2.2×10−16).

claim: As TEs lose their activity, the corresponding piRNAs erode away.
source: Here we reported that all active TEs in the chicken germ line are targeted by piRNAs, and as TEs lose their activity, the corresponding piRNAs erode away.
evidence: Figure 2C shows that piRNAs targeting inactive TEs are less abundant than those targeting active TEs (p<2.2×10−16), and Figure 2D shows that inactive TEs not targeted by piRNAs are older than those targeted by piRNAs.

claim: Avian leukosis virus (ALV) has endogenized prior to chicken domestication.
source: Avian leukosis virus (ALV) has endogenized prior to chicken domestication, remains infectious, and threatens poultry industry.
evidence: The manuscript cites that ALVE was introduced into the chicken genome following speciation but prior to domestication (Frisby et al., 1979).

claim: ALV remains infectious.
source: Avian leukosis virus (ALV) has endogenized prior to chicken domestication, remains infectious, and threatens poultry industry.
evidence: The manuscript cites that uninfected chickens sometimes spontaneously shed infectious ALV subtype E (ALVE) viruses (Varmus et al., 1972; Weiss, 2006).

claim: ALV threatens the poultry industry.
source: Avian leukosis virus (ALV) has endogenized prior to chicken domestication, remains infectious, and threatens poultry industry.
evidence: The manuscript cites that ALV infection can lead to cancer (Weiss, 2006) and that ALVJ was associated with myeloid leukosis in meat-type chickens (Smith et al., 1999) and later mutated to infect egg-laying breeds with a wide spectrum of tumors (Gao et al., 2010).

claim: Domestic fowl produce piRNAs targeting ALV from one ALV provirus that was known to render its host ALV resistant.
source: Domestic fowl produce piRNAs targeting ALV from one ALV provirus that was known to render its host ALV resistant.
evidence: Figure 4E shows that cluster 719 contains the truncated ALVE provirus (ALVE6) and produces abundant piRNAs in White Leghorn. The manuscript cites that this defective provirus has been associated with ALVE resistance (Robinson et al., 1981).

claim: The ALV proviral locus does not produce piRNAs in undomesticated wild chickens.
source: This proviral locus does not produce piRNAs in undomesticated wild chickens.
evidence: Figure 1C and Figure 4E show that Red Jungle Fowl do not produce robust ALVE piRNAs, and Figure 3B,C show that ALVE-mapping reads in Red Jungle Fowl lack strong U bias and significant Ping-Pong amplification.

claim: 73 TE families were active in White Leghorn testis.
source: We found that 73 TE families, including ALVE, were active in White Leghorn testis, and all 503 TE insertions absent in Red Jungle Fowl were derived from these TE families.
evidence: Figure 1D shows the 2×2 contingency table indicating 73 TE families with both transcription and translation, and Figure 2B confirms 73 TE families are expressed.

claim: All 503 TE insertions absent in Red Jungle Fowl were derived from the 73 active TE families.
source: We found that 73 TE families, including ALVE, were active in White Leghorn testis, and all 503 TE insertions absent in Red Jungle Fowl were derived from these TE families.
evidence: Figure 1D shows that no putative new insertion came from the 127 transcriptionally inactive TE families, and all putative new insertions came from the 73 actively transcribed TE families.

claim: More than 60% of the active TEs belonged to ERV families.
source: More than 60% of the active TEs belonged to ERV families, indicating that ERVs contribute to most TE activity in chickens.
evidence: The manuscript states that 47 out of 73 young TE families are ERVs, which is approximately 64%.

claim: ERVs contribute to most TE activity in chickens.
source: More than 60% of the active TEs belonged to ERV families, indicating that ERVs contribute to most TE activity in chickens.
evidence: The manuscript shows that 47 out of 73 active TE families are ERVs, and all new insertions come from these active families.

claim: piRNAs protect the germ line by targeting transposable elements through base-pair complementarity.
source: PIWI-interacting RNAs (piRNAs) protect the germ line by targeting transposable elements (TEs) through the base-pair complementarity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by established scientific knowledge about piRNA function.

claim: Disruption of piRNA pathways activates TEs in male and female fruit flies.
source: Disruption of piRNA pathways activates TEs in male and female fruit flies (Wilson et al., 1996; Lin and Spradling, 1997), male and female zebrafish (Houwing et al., 2008), and male mice (Kuramochi-Miyagawa et al., 2004; Carmell et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies demonstrating this effect.

claim: Disruption of piRNA pathways activates TEs in male and female zebrafish.
source: Disruption of piRNA pathways activates TEs in male and female fruit flies (Wilson et al., 1996; Lin and Spradling, 1997), male and female zebrafish (Houwing et al., 2008), and male mice (Kuramochi-Miyagawa et al., 2004; Carmell et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites Houwing et al., 2008 for this finding.

claim: Disruption of piRNA pathways activates TEs in male mice.
source: Disruption of piRNA pathways activates TEs in male and female fruit flies (Wilson et al., 1996; Lin and Spradling, 1997), male and female zebrafish (Houwing et al., 2008), and male mice (Kuramochi-Miyagawa et al., 2004; Carmell et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites Kuramochi-Miyagawa et al., 2004 and Carmell et al., 2007 for this finding.

claim: piRNAs bind a specialized sub-family of Argonaute proteins, the PIWI proteins.
source: piRNAs bind a specialized sub-family of Argonaute proteins, the PIWI proteins, which are expressed mainly in germ cells (Kumar and Carmichael, 1998; Aravin and Hannon, 2008; Farazi et al., 2008; Kim et al., 2009; Thomson and Lin, 2009; Cenik and Zamore, 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies supporting this statement.

claim: PIWI proteins are expressed mainly in germ cells.
source: piRNAs bind a specialized sub-family of Argonaute proteins, the PIWI proteins, which are expressed mainly in germ cells (Kumar and Carmichael, 1998; Aravin and Hannon, 2008; Farazi et al., 2008; Kim et al., 2009; Thomson and Lin, 2009; Cenik and Zamore, 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies and also shows in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B that CILI and CIWI are expressed exclusively in testis.

claim: PIWI proteins catalyze an endonucleolytic cleavage between the 10th and 11th positions of the RNA target relative to the piRNA 5´end.
source: PIWI proteins catalyze an endonucleolytic cleavage between the 10th and 11th positions of the RNA target relative to the piRNA 5´end.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and is supported by established knowledge about PIWI protein function.

claim: The cleaved product can be loaded into another PIWI protein becoming a secondary piRNA, resulting in a 'Ping-Pong' loop that amplifies antisense TE piRNAs.
source: The cleaved product can then be loaded into another PIWI protein becoming a secondary piRNA. This results in a 'Ping-Pong' loop that amplifies antisense TE piRNAs (Brennecke et al., 2007; Gunawardane et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites Brennecke et al., 2007 and Gunawardane et al., 2007 for this mechanism.

claim: The only known mechanism of new piRNA acquisition comes from studies of fruit flies, in which a TE inserts into an actively expressed piRNA cluster.
source: The only known mechanism of new piRNA acquisition comes from studies of fruit flies, in which a TE inserts into an actively expressed piRNA cluster (Khurana et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites Khurana et al., 2011 for this mechanism.

claim: Active piRNA-producing loci represent only a tiny fraction of the genome.
source: However, considering that active piRNA-producing loci represent only a tiny fraction of the genome, and that no preference for insertions of TEs into piRNA-producing loci has been reported (Kumar and Chen, 2012), other piRNA acquisition mechanisms remain to be discovered.
evidence: The manuscript shows that 1633 piRNA clusters account for 0.88% of the chicken genome, supporting this statement.

claim: No preference for insertions of TEs into piRNA-producing loci has been reported.
source: However, considering that active piRNA-producing loci represent only a tiny fraction of the genome, and that no preference for insertions of TEs into piRNA-producing loci has been reported (Kumar and Chen, 2012), other piRNA acquisition mechanisms remain to be discovered.
evidence: The manuscript cites Kumar and Chen, 2012 for this statement, and Figure 1D shows that none of the new ALVE insertions in White Leghorn were found within or near the 1633 identified piRNA-producing loci.

claim: Chicken ERVs are more active than other TEs in the chicken genome.
source: Compared to other TEs in the chicken genome, including the ancient CR1 superfamily (Vandergon and Reitman, 1994) and DNA transposons, and largely absent short interspersed nuclear elements (SINEs) (International Chicken Genome Sequencing Consortium, 2004), chicken ERVs are more active and have led to phenotypic changes like blue egg-shells (Wang et al., 2013) and late feathering (Boyce-Jacino et al., 1989).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies and shows that 47 out of 73 active TE families are ERVs.

claim: Chicken ERVs have led to phenotypic changes like blue egg-shells.
source: Compared to other TEs in the chicken genome, including the ancient CR1 superfamily (Vandergon and Reitman, 1994) and DNA transposons, and largely absent short interspersed nuclear elements (SINEs) (International Chicken Genome Sequencing Consortium, 2004), chicken ERVs are more active and have led to phenotypic changes like blue egg-shells (Wang et al., 2013) and late feathering (Boyce-Jacino et al., 1989).
evidence: The manuscript cites Wang et al., 2013 for this phenotypic change.

claim: Chicken ERVs have led to phenotypic changes like late feathering.
source: Compared to other TEs in the chicken genome, including the ancient CR1 superfamily (Vandergon and Reitman, 1994) and DNA transposons, and largely absent short interspersed nuclear elements (SINEs) (International Chicken Genome Sequencing Consortium, 2004), chicken ERVs are more active and have led to phenotypic changes like blue egg-shells (Wang et al., 2013) and late feathering (Boyce-Jacino et al., 1989).
evidence: The manuscript cites Boyce-Jacino et al., 1989 for this phenotypic change.

claim: ALV was the first ERV to be discovered.
source: Avian leukosis virus (ALV) was the first ERV to be discovered (Temin, 1964; Weiss, 1969; Baluda, 1972).
evidence: The manuscript cites Temin, 1964; Weiss, 1969; and Baluda, 1972 for this historical fact.

claim: Uninfected chickens sometimes spontaneously shed infectious ALV subtype E (ALVE) viruses.
source: Uninfected chickens sometimes spontaneously shed infectious ALV subtype E (ALVE) viruses (Varmus et al., 1972; Weiss, 2006), and the infection can lead to cancer (Weiss, 2006).
evidence: The manuscript cites Varmus et al., 1972 and Weiss, 2006 for this observation.

claim: ALVE infection can lead to cancer.
source: Uninfected chickens sometimes spontaneously shed infectious ALV subtype E (ALVE) viruses (Varmus et al., 1972; Weiss, 2006), and the infection can lead to cancer (Weiss, 2006).
evidence: The manuscript cites Weiss, 2006 for this statement.

claim: ALV acquisition of a host oncogene, SRC, generated a more acute transforming virus, Rous sarcoma virus (RSV).
source: ALV acquisition of a host oncogene, SRC, generated a more acute transforming virus, Rous sarcoma virus (RSV) (Stehelin et al., 1976).
evidence: The manuscript cites Stehelin et al., 1976 for this statement.

claim: Recombination between ALVE and EAV-HP has created ALV subtype J (ALVJ).
source: Recombination between ALVE and EAV-HP—a member of the endogenous avian retrovirus (EAV) family, has created ALV subtype J (ALVJ), a new subgroup of ALVs that were associated with myeloid leukosis in meat-type chickens (Smith et al., 1999).
evidence: The manuscript cites Smith et al., 1999 for this statement.

claim: ALVJ was associated with myeloid leukosis in meat-type chickens.
source: Recombination between ALVE and EAV-HP—a member of the endogenous avian retrovirus (EAV) family, has created ALV subtype J (ALVJ), a new subgroup of ALVs that were associated with myeloid leukosis in meat-type chickens (Smith et al., 1999).
evidence: The manuscript cites Smith et al., 1999 for this statement.

claim: After spreading to China in 2002, ALVJ mutated to infect egg-laying breeds with a wide spectrum of tumors.
source: After spreading to China in 2002, ALVJ mutated to infect egg-laying breeds with a wide spectrum of tumors (Gao et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites Gao et al., 2010 for this statement.

claim: White Leghorn is the most popular egg-laying breed.
source: Here, we identified the ERV activity and piRNA-producing loci in White Leghorn, the most popular egg-laying breed, dissected the interplay between ERVs and piRNAs, and traced the origination of recently acquired piRNAs in undomesticated wild chickens, Red Jungle Fowl (Eriksson et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction.

claim: White Leghorn lays an average of 280 eggs per year.
source: White Leghorn lays an average of 280 eggs per year (Bao et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript cites Bao et al., 2008 for this statement.

claim: The late-feathering trait is linked to a fully infectious ALVE provirus (known as ev21) on the Z chromosome.
source: Breeders have used the late-feathering trait as a convenient marker to select female layers at hatch (Boyce-Jacino et al., 1989); however, this trait is linked to a fully infectious ALVE provirus (known as ev21) on the Z chromosome, which causes decreased performance (Smith and Fadly, 1988; Fadly and Smith, 1997).
evidence: The manuscript cites Smith and Fadly, 1988 and Fadly and Smith, 1997 for this statement.

claim: The ev21 ALVE provirus causes decreased performance in chickens.
source: Breeders have used the late-feathering trait as a convenient marker to select female layers at hatch (Boyce-Jacino et al., 1989); however, this trait is linked to a fully infectious ALVE provirus (known as ev21) on the Z chromosome, which causes decreased performance (Smith and Fadly, 1988; Fadly and Smith, 1997).
evidence: The manuscript cites Smith and Fadly, 1988 and Fadly and Smith, 1997 for this statement.

claim: Chicken ERV families were ubiquitously expressed across 12 tissues.
source: Comparison of RNA-seq data from 12 tissues (Brawand et al., 2011) indicated that chicken ERV families were ubiquitously expressed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 1A shows ERV expression across different tissues.

claim: The highest ERV expression was in testis and ovary.
source: Because the highest expression was in testis and ovary—the only tissues where their expansion can become heritable (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), we decided to perform polysome profile analysis to determine whether ERVs were also being translated in testis.
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 1A shows the highest ERV expression in testis and ovary.

claim: CR1-B, CR1-F, EAV-HP, and ALVE transcripts co-sedimented with polysomes.
source: CR1-B, CR1-F, EAV-HP, and ALVE transcripts co-sedimented with polysomes.
evidence: Figure 1A shows the distribution of these transcripts across polysome fractions.

claim: CR1-B, CR1-F, EAV-HP, and ALVE insertions are transcribed and translated in testis.
source: These profiling results suggest that CR1-B, CR1-F, EAV and ALVE insertions are transcribed and translated in testis.
evidence: Figure 1A shows polysome profiling results, and Figure 1B shows ribosome profiling data.

claim: The ribosome-bound fraction of mRNA is protected from RNase digestion in vitro.
source: Ribosome profiling is based on the facts that the ribosome-bound fraction of mRNA is protected from RNase digestion in vitro (Steitz, 1969), and that the subsequent genome-wide sequencing of ribosome-protected fragments (RPFs) provides a snapshot of in vivo translation (Ingolia et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites Steitz, 1969 for this fact.

claim: Genome-wide sequencing of ribosome-protected fragments (RPFs) provides a snapshot of in vivo translation.
source: Ribosome profiling is based on the facts that the ribosome-bound fraction of mRNA is protected from RNase digestion in vitro (Steitz, 1969), and that the subsequent genome-wide sequencing of ribosome-protected fragments (RPFs) provides a snapshot of in vivo translation (Ingolia et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites Ingolia et al., 2009 for this statement.

claim: RPF sizes in chicken from coding DNA sequences (CDS) ranged from 26–32 nt.
source: Similar to reported RPF sizes in mammals, the RPF sizes in chicken from coding DNA sequences (CDS) ranged from 26–32 nt (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 3B shows the length distribution of RPFs.

claim: RPF reads mapping to CDS regions accounted for 96% of the RPFs that mapped to entire mRNA transcripts.
source: While RNA-seq reads were distributed throughout the entire set of mRNA transcripts, RPF reads were enriched in CDS regions (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C), and RPFs that mapped to CDS regions accounted for 96% of the RPFs that mapped to entire mRNA transcripts.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: RPF reads mapping to open read frames displayed an obvious three-nt periodicity.
source: The RPF reads mapping to open read frames displayed an obvious three-nt periodicity (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D), reflecting the triplet nature of the genetic code during translation elongation.
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 3D shows the discrete Fourier transformation demonstrating three-nt periodicity.

claim: The ribosome density of each TE family correlated with their steady-state RNA levels (ρ = 0.82, p<2.2×10−16).
source: The ribosome density of each TE family correlated with their steady-state RNA levels (ρ = 0.82, p<2.2×10−16) (Figure 1B).
evidence: Figure 1B shows the scatter plot demonstrating this correlation.

claim: The median translational efficiency of ERVs was around 1/10 of the median translation efficiency of mRNAs that were expressed in testis.
source: The median translational efficiency (ratio of ribosome density to transcript abundance) of ERVs was around 1/10 of the median translation efficiency of mRNAs that were expressed in testis.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on analysis of Figure 1B data.

claim: ALVE RPF reads displayed codon periodicity.
source: These ALVE RPF reads displayed a length distribution that was similar to that of RPFs from CDS regions (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B), and they displayed codon periodicity (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 3D shows the codon periodicity for ALVE RPFs.

claim: ALVE RPFs were distributed throughout the entire ALVE transcripts but with higher abundance at gag and env than at pol.
source: These RPFs were distributed throughout the entire ALVE transcripts but with higher abundance at gag and env than at pol (Figure 1C).
evidence: Figure 1C shows the distribution of RPFs across ALVE.

claim: Most transcribed TEs were also translated (the two events, transcription and translation, were significantly associated: Fisher's exact test, p<2.2×10−16).
source: Most transcribed TEs were also translated (the two events, transcription and translation, were significantly associated: Fisher's exact test, p<2.2×10−16; Figure 1D).
evidence: Figure 1D shows the 2×2 contingency table for Fisher's exact test.

claim: RPFs were detected in 71 of 73 TE families that were transcribed (97.3%).
source: We detected RPFs in 71 of 73 TE families that were transcribed (97.3%).
evidence: This is stated in the text based on the ribosome profiling analysis.

claim: 503 putative TE insertions, absent in Red Jungle Fowl, were distributed throughout the chicken genome.
source: 503 putative TE insertions, absent in Red Jungle Fowl, were distributed throughout the chicken genome (Figure 1D, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Figure 1D shows the Circos plot of putative new insertions, and Supplementary file 1 lists them.

claim: No putative new insertion came from the 127 transcriptionally inactive TE families.
source: No putative new insertion came from the 127 transcriptionally inactive TE families (Figure 1D), confirming their inactive state.
evidence: Figure 1D shows the 2×2 contingency table indicating 0 new insertions from inactive TEs.

claim: All putative new insertions came from the 73 actively transcribed TE families.
source: All putative new insertions came from the 73 actively transcribed TE families.
evidence: Figure 1D shows that all new insertions are from the 73 active TE families.

claim: TE piRNAs accounted for 7.8% of total piRNAs in adult testis of White Leghorn.
source: Using small RNA-seq data from the adult testis of White Leghorn (Li et al., 2013), we detected abundant TE piRNAs, which accounted for 7.8% of total piRNAs, and exhibited a size range peaking at 24–25 nt.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on small RNA-seq analysis.

claim: TE piRNAs exhibited a size range peaking at 24–25 nt.
source: Using small RNA-seq data from the adult testis of White Leghorn (Li et al., 2013), we detected abundant TE piRNAs, which accounted for 7.8% of total piRNAs, and exhibited a size range peaking at 24–25 nt.
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1A shows the length distribution of TE piRNAs.

claim: TE piRNAs were resistant to oxidation.
source: These small RNAs were resistant to oxidation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1B shows the scatter plot comparing piRNA abundance in total vs oxidized libraries.

claim: TE piRNAs typically began with uracil (61.6% of species and 66.7% of reads).
source: Like piRNAs in other species, these TE piRNAs typically began with uracil (61.6% of species and 66.7% of reads, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1C shows the sequence logo with 1st U bias.

claim: Almost equal numbers of piRNAs mapped to sense versus antisense strands (median ratio of sense to antisense piRNAs was 1.2).
source: Almost equal numbers of piRNAs mapped to sense versus antisense strands (median ratio of sense to antisense piRNAs was 1.2) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), and there was an adenine bias at the 10th position (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), indicating that secondary piRNAs are generated (Brennecke et al., 2007; Gunawardane et al., 2007).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1D shows the scatter plot of sense vs antisense piRNA abundance.

claim: There was an adenine bias at the 10th position of TE piRNAs.
source: Almost equal numbers of piRNAs mapped to sense versus antisense strands (median ratio of sense to antisense piRNAs was 1.2) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), and there was an adenine bias at the 10th position (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), indicating that secondary piRNAs are generated (Brennecke et al., 2007; Gunawardane et al., 2007).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1C shows the sequence logo with 10th A bias.

claim: A significant Z score at a distance of 10 nt was detected, a signature of robust Ping-Pong amplification.
source: We detected a significant Z score at a distance of 10 nt, a signature of robust Ping-Pong amplification (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E) (Brennecke et al., 2007; Gunawardane et al., 2007).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 1E shows the 5´−5´ overlap analysis with a peak at 10 nt.

claim: A piRNA mediated silencing pathway against TEs is active in the chicken germ line.
source: These findings indicate that a piRNA mediated silencing pathway against TEs is active in the chicken germ line.
evidence: This is inferred from the detection of authentic piRNAs with characteristic features (length, oxidation resistance, 1st U bias, 10th A bias, Ping-Pong amplification).

claim: The expression of piRNAs that target each TE family correlated with overall TE expression (ρ = 0.81, p<2.2 × 10−16).
source: The expression of piRNAs that target each TE family correlated with overall TE expression (ρ = 0.81, p<2.2 × 10−16, Figure 2A; the two events were significantly associated: Fisher's exact test, p<2.2 × 10−16, Figure 2B), although there were exceptions.
evidence: Figure 2A shows the scatter plot demonstrating this correlation.

claim: All the 73 actively expressed TE families were targeted by piRNAs.
source: All the 73 actively expressed TE families were targeted by piRNAs.
evidence: Figure 2B shows that all 73 TE families with RNA-seq >1 fpkm also have piRNA >1 rpkm.

claim: Most inactive TEs (108 families) are not targeted by piRNAs.
source: Most inactive TEs (108 families) are not targeted by piRNAs; interestingly, 19 inactive TEs are targeted by piRNAs.
evidence: Figure 2B shows that 108 TE families have both low RNA-seq and low piRNA expression.

claim: 19 inactive TEs are targeted by piRNAs.
source: Most inactive TEs (108 families) are not targeted by piRNAs; interestingly, 19 inactive TEs are targeted by piRNAs.
evidence: Figure 2B shows that 19 TE families have low RNA-seq but high piRNA expression.

claim: piRNAs that target inactive TEs are less abundant than the piRNAs that target active TEs (p<2.2×10−16).
source: Those piRNAs that target inactive TEs exhibit the authentic piRNA length distribution, resistance to oxidation, and first position (1st) U bias (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B), but they are less abundant than the piRNAs that target active TEs (p<2.2×10−16) (Figure 2C).
evidence: Figure 2C shows box plots comparing piRNA abundance between young, medium, and old TEs.

claim: piRNAs that target active TEs display a robust Ping-Pong amplification with a median Z score of 12.2.
source: piRNAs that target active TEs display a robust Ping-Pong amplification with a median Z score of 12.2; whereas, the piRNAs that target the inactive TEs do not show significant Ping-Pong amplification (median Z score of 0.41) (Figure 2C; Z-score >3.3 corresponds to p<0.01), although both sense and antisense TE piRNAs are produced in equal abundance (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Figure 2C shows box plots comparing Ping-Pong scores between young, medium, and old TEs.

claim: piRNAs that target inactive TEs do not show significant Ping-Pong amplification (median Z score of 0.41).
source: piRNAs that target active TEs display a robust Ping-Pong amplification with a median Z score of 12.2; whereas, the piRNAs that target the inactive TEs do not show significant Ping-Pong amplification (median Z score of 0.41) (Figure 2C; Z-score >3.3 corresponds to p<0.01), although both sense and antisense TE piRNAs are produced in equal abundance (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Figure 2C shows box plots comparing Ping-Pong scores between young, medium, and old TEs.

claim: All active TEs that were targeted by piRNAs are recent invaders of the chicken genome.
source: We found that all active TEs that were targeted by piRNAs are recent invaders of the chicken genome.
evidence: Figure 2D shows that young TEs are specific to Gallus gallus or other Gallus genera.

claim: ERVs comprised most of the young TEs (47 out of 73 families).
source: These young TEs are specific to Gallus gallus or other Gallus genera. ERVs comprised most of these young TEs (47 out of 73 families), which is consistent with the observations that non-ERV TEs lack recent activity in chickens (International Chicken Genome Sequencing Consortium, 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the text based on analysis of TE ages.

claim: More than 90% of inactive TEs that were not targeted by piRNAs had invaded the chicken genome before birds and other amniotes diverged.
source: More than 90% of inactive TEs that were not targeted by piRNAs had invaded the chicken genome before birds and other amniotes diverged.
evidence: Figure 2D shows that old TEs invaded before Amniota divergence.

claim: The 19 inactive TEs that were targeted by piRNAs were of medium age, exhibiting invasion times that were distinct from both old and young TEs (χ2, p≤2.5×10−9).
source: We found that the 19 inactive TEs that were targeted by piRNAs were of medium age, exhibiting invasion times that were distinct from both old and young TEs (Figure 2D, χ2, p≤2.5×10−9).
evidence: Figure 2D shows the histogram of TE ages for young, medium, and old TEs.

claim: piRNA expression reflects TE age—young TEs are targeted by abundant piRNAs, while TE inactivation leads to the erosion of piRNA production.
source: From these data, we conclude that piRNA expression reflects TE age—young TEs are targeted by abundant piRNAs, while TE inactivation leads to the erosion of piRNA production.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the data showing correlation between TE age and piRNA abundance (Figure 2C,D).

claim: A rapid turnover of chicken piRNA sequences reflects contemporary TE activity.
source: Our data imply that a rapid turnover of chicken piRNA sequences reflects contemporary TE activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that piRNA expression correlates with TE activity and age.

claim: Abundant piRNAs mapping to ALVE were detected in adult rooster testis.
source: piRNAs have not previously been shown to suppress any infectious virus—exogenous or endogenous—in vertebrates; yet, we unexpectedly detected abundant piRNAs mapping to ALVE in adult rooster testis (Figure 3A).
evidence: Figure 3A shows the length distribution of ALVE-mapping small RNAs.

claim: ALVE-mapping reads peaked at 25 nt and were resistant to oxidation.
source: These ALVE-mapping reads, which peaked at 25 nt were resistant to oxidation, indicating that they were authentic piRNAs.
evidence: Figure 3A shows the length distribution peaking at 25 nt, and oxidation resistance is mentioned in the text.

claim: ALVE piRNAs mapped to both strands of ALVE, spanning env and the 3´ half of pol.
source: These piRNAs mapped to both strands of ALVE (Figure 1C), spanning env and the 3´ half of pol.
evidence: Figure 1C shows the distribution of piRNAs across ALVE.

claim: The sense ALVE piRNAs exhibited a typical 1st U bias.
source: The sense piRNAs exhibited a typical 1st U bias, and the antisense piRNAs exhibited a 10th A bias (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C), indicating production of secondary piRNAs.
evidence: Figure 3B shows the sequence logo with 1st U bias for sense ALVE piRNAs.

claim: The antisense ALVE piRNAs exhibited a 10th A bias.
source: The sense piRNAs exhibited a typical 1st U bias, and the antisense piRNAs exhibited a 10th A bias (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C), indicating production of secondary piRNAs.
evidence: Figure 3B shows the sequence logo with 10th A bias for antisense ALVE piRNAs.

claim: Robust Ping-Pong amplification signals were detected in ALVE piRNAs.
source: Indeed, robust Ping-Pong amplification signals were detected in ALVE piRNAs (Figure 3B).
evidence: Figure 3C shows the 5´−5´ overlap analysis with a significant Z-score at 10 nt for ALVE piRNAs in White Leghorn.

claim: ALVE piRNAs were produced to an abundance of 188 parts per million reads mapped to the genome (ppm).
source: ALVE piRNAs were produced to an abundance of 188 parts per million reads mapped to the genome (ppm), which was roughly half the abundance of EAV-HP piRNAs (359 ppm).
evidence: This is stated in the text based on small RNA-seq analysis.

claim: EAV-HP piRNAs were produced to an abundance of 359 ppm.
source: ALVE piRNAs were produced to an abundance of 188 parts per million reads mapped to the genome (ppm), which was roughly half the abundance of EAV-HP piRNAs (359 ppm).
evidence: This is stated in the text based on small RNA-seq analysis.

claim: Roughly 3000 ALVE piRNA species were detected.
source: Because small RNAs recognize their targets without complete sequence complementarity (Bartel, 2009), the roughly 3000 ALVE piRNA species detected can recognize mutated ALVE, which thus might explain why other ALV family members failed to endogenize.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on small RNA-seq analysis.

claim: ALVE was introduced into the chicken genome following speciation but prior to domestication.

source: Using our previously developed dynamic programming algorithm (Li et al., 2013), in total, we identified 1633 piRNA clusters that accounted for 0.88% of the chicken genome, and explained 87.3% of total piRNA reads and 81.1% of uniquely mapping piRNAs (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the text, and Figure 4A shows the cumulative distribution.

claim: Chicken piRNAs were produced from both strands of piRNA clusters.
source: Unlike divergently and uni-directionally transcribed mouse piRNA-producing loci, we observed that chicken piRNAs were produced from both strands of piRNA clusters (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) as reported previously (Li et al., 2013; Chirn et al., 2015), and were derived from convergently transcribed precursors detected by our RNA-seq data (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Over 70% of clusters (1173 out of 1633) included uniquely mapping piRNAs transcribed from either strand at a level of greater than 10% of total uniquely mapping piRNAs from that cluster.

evidence: This is stated in the text based on analysis of piRNA cluster data.

claim: Most chicken piRNA-producing loci are transcribed from both strands, and both transcripts are processed into piRNAs.
source: Based on these findings, we conclude that most chicken piRNA-producing loci are transcribed from both strands, and both transcripts are processed into piRNAs.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the observation that over 70% of clusters produce piRNAs from both strands.

claim: The median abundance of piRNA precursors in the testis was 2.6 fpkm.

claim: The expression of two PIWI genes, CILI and CIWI, was only detected in testis.

claim: The detection of piRNA precursors and PIWI mRNAs exclusively in testis is consistent with their role in protecting the germ-line genome.
source: The detection of piRNA precursors and PIWI mRNAs exclusively in testis is consistent with their role in protecting the germ-line genome.
evidence: This is inferred from the tissue-specific expression pattern.

claim: The lack of detection of PIWI mRNAs and piRNA precursors in ovary suggests that chicken piRNA pathways display sexual dimorphism.

claim: None of the new ALVE insertions in White Leghorn were found within or near the 1633 identified piRNA-producing loci.

None of the new ALVE insertions in White Leghorn were found within or near the 1633 identified piRNA-producing loci (Supplementary file 1).

claim: In White Leghorn, the divergent piRNA clusters accounted for only 3.7% of uniquely mapping piRNAs.

claim: Chicken has two PIWI proteins, CILI and CIWI.
source: CILI and CIWI are the two PIWI proteins in chickens (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 2 shows the phylogenetic tree of PIWI proteins including chicken CILI and CIWI.
